verdict.reasoning: Onset and character: Patient says diarrhea started three days ago (“It was three days ago now”) and was watery then very loose (“it's very loose but it started as being very watery”). Frequency: “Today alone, I've been at least four time,” so ‘more than 4’ slightly overstates but is a reasonable approximation of lost count and “at least four.”
Feverish: Patient reports “I've been running a serious temperature. I'm literally boiling.” Not measured: When asked if she checked with a thermometer, she replies “No, 'cause I've not got one.”

Nausea/vomiting and contents: Patient says “I've been throwing up. I can't seem to be able to keep anything in me. Not even water, not even my tea, not even any liquid stuff. I've just been throwing up everything.” Timing: When asked when she was last sick: “just after trying… to have breakfast this morning, so maybe about two hours ago.”

Location/tenderness: She states pain is “towards my navel area… I can't touch my navel area. It's just so sore. And it gets, yeah, it's almost like the center of my navel,” which is periumbilical and very tender to touch. Intermittent and associated with urge to defecate: In response to whether the pain comes and goes, she says “Yes, it does come. When it comes, I feel this strong urge to go to the loo,” supporting intermittent, cramp-like pain with urge to defecate.

Voiding okay: When asked about passing water, she says “Yeah, I've been, I've been, yeah, urinating OK.” Last void: “when did you last pass urine?” — “an hour ago.” Color unknown: When asked urine color she replies, “To be honest, I have a look so I really couldn't say,” indicating unknown color.

Blood in stool/urine: Doctor asks, “any blood in the stool or in the urine that you've noticed?” Patient: “No blood.” Rash: “Have you had any other symptoms at the moment, like rash?” Patient: “No, no rash.”

Baseline bowels: She says, “my bowels is normally fine. I would normally go to the toilet every day. You know, in the morning, just once,” and when asked about episodes of diarrhea or constipation normally: “No.” This supports daily formed stool with no prior diarrhea or constipation.

Sick contact and no travel: When asked about a trigger or travel, she says “No, but then, um, my, um my brother, um, has actually been having similar symptoms… for the past, um, few days as well, and he does say like everyone in school's got this,” and confirms contact: Doctor: “So you've been in contact with him, have you?” Patient: “Yes.” She previously answered “No” to “Have you been abroad anywhere?”

Abdominal history/surgery: Doctor asks “any surgery before, or abdominal problems, or any other medical issues?” Patient: “Well, apart from the fact that this one is giving me abdominal pains, no previous abdominal pains before.” No surgeries or other abdominal problems are mentioned, supporting absence. Dysmenorrhea: She adds, “Obviously I get the odd, um, you know, menstrual cramps and all that but, you know, that comes and goes,” consistent with dysmenorrhea.
Regular meds: “Well, I, I take my, my vitamins, vitamin D, every day. That's about, that's about all that I regularly take.”
Ibuprofen use: “for my menstrual cramps, when they come, maybe I might take a, a, an ibuprofen just to ease the pain.” This supports ibuprofen as needed for menstrual cramps.

ORS use and poor retention: She says she tried “the ORS, the, the salt sugar ORS… mix,” and when asked how often: “I've taken that, I've taken that, like, um, three times a day for the past two days.” She also states, “I've been vomiting literally everything I take, so, so I doubt that even that had, had the chance to work,” indicating most is vomited.

Smoking: “Well, I don't smoke.” Alcohol: “but, you know, I have a pint from time to time.” Drugs: “And do you take any other drugs?” — “No. Like I said, I only take, um, vitamins.” Occupation: She states “A graphics designer.” (equivalent to graphic designer).

Living situation: “I live with my brother and my mum.” Work impact: When asked if she had to miss work: “Well, yes, I've had to actually work from home today. I'm working from home today because I can't, I can't be out for work.”

The doctor explicitly states a likely diagnosis: “it sounds like it might be some, an infectious gastroenteritis that you've got, which is usually caused by a virus.” The components—3 days of watery/loose diarrhea (supported in cc-001), nausea/vomiting (hpi-002), subjective fever (hpi-001), periumbilical cramps (hpi-003), sick contact with similar symptoms (hpi-007), and no blood (hpi-005)—are all directly described in the transcript.

Risk of dehydration: Doctor explains “we should also check that you're not getting dehydrated, because if you're, if you're not keeping fluid down, then you can get dehydrated,” and notes ongoing vomiting and limited oral tolerance. Yet she is “still… urinating OK” and last passed urine “an hour ago,” supporting ongoing but at-risk hydration status.

Urgent clinic assessment and stool sample: Doctor says, “I think it's probably important to get a sample of the stool, so we can make sure that you haven't got a nasty bacterial infection,” and “we should see you so that we can check your hydration and, um, get that sample sent off as soon as possible.” Later: “we can make you an urgent appointment, um, and then you can, you can get the sample sent off and we can check your hydration.”

Continue ORS, tiny frequent sips: Doctor advises, “you need to carry on with your rehydration salts, and just have very small amounts,” and later, “If you keep drinking, keep going with the rehydration salts. Just tiny sips constantly… so that your stomach doesn't get overfilled and, and you vomit.” Aim is maintaining hydration/urine output, which is explicitly discussed earlier.

Diet advice: Doctor says, “just have very simple food, if you're gonna have anything, like toast or biscuit or something really light like that. Avoid, um, fruit, vegetables, uh, milk, anything like that, which might just make it worse.” This matches recommendation for simple foods and avoiding fruit, vegetables, and milk.

Safety net: Doctor advises, “if, in the meantime, you're feeling more unwell, then we would get you seen urgently in A and E,” and “So you can call us back in the meantime.” Combined with instructions about keeping fluids down, this supports calling back if symptoms worsen and attending A&E if more unwell or unable to keep fluids down.

Booking via support line: Doctor states, “So you'll have to book an appointment through the support line.” The appointment was described as urgent earlier, so ‘book urgent appointment via support line’ is consistent.
